questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the sharper version of the Flow-vs-Apex tradeoff, beyond 'Flow is simple, Apex is complex'?
options: Which tool costs more in Salesforce licensing fees
Who can actually own and safely maintain the result afterward, and what happens when the logic needs to scale or branch beyond what the declarative tool was built for
Whether the automation runs on a custom object versus a standard object
Whether the org has purchased the Lightning Platform Plus license
questions.explain: The lesson frames the real tradeoff around ownership and maintainability over time, not just surface-level complexity -- a sprawling Flow can become just as unmaintainable as bad Apex, just without version control or unit tests to catch a regression.

questions.q: What is an 'invocable method,' and why does it matter to this tradeoff?
options: A type of Flow element that replaces the need for Apex entirely
A governor limit that caps how many Apex classes a Flow can reference
An Apex method exposed so a Flow can call it, enabling a hybrid design that keeps orchestration and visibility in Flow while handing one specific piece of logic to Apex
A Salesforce setting that disables Flow when Apex is present on the same object
questions.explain: Invocable methods are exactly what makes the hybrid pattern possible: Flow calls into Apex for the piece that's too complex, too high-volume, or too much in need of test coverage to build declaratively, while the rest of the process stays visible and admin-maintainable in Flow.

questions.q: Which of the following does this lesson identify as a concrete signal that should push a decision toward Apex rather than Flow?
options: The automation only needs to run occasionally against a small number of records
The business stakeholders want to be able to visually trace the logic themselves
The team maintaining the automation consists entirely of admins with no developers
The logic needs to run cleanly against high data volumes or requires careful recursion-guarding that's fragile to build declaratively
questions.explain: High-volume, recursion-sensitive logic is a strong fit for Apex's explicit control over bulkification and governor-limit management -- the other three options actually point toward Flow instead.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say Apex supports more rigorous change management than Flow, as the tools are generally used?
options: Because Apex can be covered by genuine automated unit tests run on every deployment, caught in code review, and tracked with a real diff history, while Flow's comparable testing discipline is less mature
Because Apex cannot be deployed without a full sandbox refresh
Because Flow does not support version control of any kind
Because Apex automatically generates its own documentation
questions.explain: The lesson specifically credits Apex's automated test coverage, code review practices, and version-controlled diff history as the rigor advantage -- Flow has versioning, but the surrounding testing discipline is comparatively immature.

questions.q: What does this lesson recommend as a 'good hybrid' design between Flow and Apex?
options: Rewriting every Flow in an org as Apex regardless of complexity

Keeping orchestration and business-rule visibility in Flow, and having the Flow call an invocable Apex method for the one piece of logic too complex, high-volume, or test-critical to build declaratively
Running Flow and Apex as two entirely separate, unrelated automations on the same object with no coordination
Avoiding Apex entirely and only using Flow, regardless of the automation's complexity
questions.explain: This hybrid gets the maintainability and visibility of Flow for the parts that benefit from it, and the control and rigor of Apex for just the part that actually needs it, without forcing the whole feature onto one side of the tradeoff.
